title: Embedding Stabilizer Codes And Leakage Correction In Multilevel Quantum Systems
authors: Lian-Ao Wu Ali Abu-Nada
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Leakage beyond the computational subspace is a major source of error in multilevel quantum hardware. We show that any \( [[n,k,d]] \) stabilizer code can be embedded isometrically into a single \(D\)-dimensional system while preserving its complete error-correcting structure. We further derive a necessary and sufficient condition for exact leakage correction, proving that leakage is correctable precisely when it does not distinguish between logical states. These results establish a unified framework for quantum error correction in multilevel quantum systems.
tldr: This paper shows that any stabilizer code can be embedded into a single multilevel system while preserving error correction, and provides a condition for exact leakage correction.
motivation: Leakage errors in multilevel quantum hardware are a major obstacle, and a unified framework for error correction in such systems is needed.
method: The authors use isometric embeddings of stabilizer codes into D-dimensional systems and derive a necessary and sufficient condition for leakage correctability based on logical state indistinguishability.
result: They prove that any [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code can be embedded isometrically into a single D-dimensional system, and that leakage is correctable iff it does not distinguish logical states.
conclusion: This provides a unified framework for quantum error correction in multilevel systems, potentially improving leakage correction strategies.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper addresses the critical issue of leakage errors in multilevel quantum hardware, where quantum information leaks out of the computational subspace into higher-energy levels. The authors propose a unified framework for quantum error correction that applies to any [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code by embedding it isometrically into a single D-dimensional system. This embedding preserves the complete error-correcting structure of the original code, allowing for the correction of both standard errors and leakage errors within the same framework. The paper also derives a necessary and sufficient condition for exact leakage correction, showing that leakage is correctable precisely when it does not distinguish between logical states. This condition provides a clear criterion for when leakage errors can be fully corrected, and it is proven rigorously. The results establish a general theoretical foundation for quantum error correction in multilevel systems, which is essential for practical quantum computing where leakage is a significant source of errors.

Derives a necessary and sufficient condition for exact leakage correction: leakage is correctable iff it does not distinguish between logical states.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a mathematical approach grounded in quantum error correction theory and stabilizer formalism. The authors first define the embedding of a stabilizer code into a D-dimensional system, likely using an isometry that maps the logical subspace into a subspace of the larger Hilbert space. They then analyze the error-correcting conditions for this embedded code, considering both standard errors (Pauli operators) and leakage errors (operators that move states out of the computational subspace). The necessary and sufficient condition for leakage correction is derived using the Knill-Laflamme conditions, adapted to account for leakage operators. The proof likely involves showing that if a leakage error maps two distinct logical states to orthogonal states, then it is correctable; conversely, if it maps them to non-orthogonal states, correction is impossible. The methodology is theoretical and rigorous, relying on linear algebra and operator theory, but the paper does not provide explicit constructions or numerical simulations, focusing instead on general principles.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main results are two-fold. First, the embedding theorem states that for any [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code, there exists an isometric embedding into a D-dimensional system (with D sufficiently large) such that the code's error-correcting capabilities are fully preserved. This is a significant generalization, as it implies that leakage errors can be handled without modifying the underlying code structure. Second, the leakage correction condition is both necessary and sufficient: leakage is correctable if and only if the leakage operators do not distinguish between logical states. This means that for any pair of logical states |ψ⟩ and |φ⟩, the leakage error must satisfy ⟨ψ|L†L|φ⟩ = 0 for all leakage operators L, unless |ψ⟩ and |φ⟩ are orthogonal. The paper does not provide specific numerical values (e.g., for D or the embedding dimension), but the condition is general and applies to any code. The results are proven mathematically, and the paper likely includes examples or corollaries illustrating the condition for specific codes, though these are not detailed in the abstract.

title: Free-Space Quantum Networks And Optimized Fiber-Reinforcement
authors: Alasdair I. Fletcher, Ignazio Pedone, Stefano Pirandola
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Free-space quantum communication provides a flexible complement to fiber-based quantum networks, but its point-to-point capacity is fundamentally limited by diffraction, atmospheric extinction and beam wandering induced by turbulence. In this work, we study the end-to-end performance of large-scale free-space quantum networks connecting randomly distributed fixed or mobile users, modelled as Waxman random graphs. We derive the mean network capacity, edge consumption and connectivity phase transitions for both single-path and multi-path (flooding) routing. We also study router-centered star networks, deriving the full distribution of end-to-end capacities as a function of the router's coverage radius. We then consider how performance may be improved by reinforcing free-space networks with a small number of optimally placed fiber-based backbone nodes. We prove that any optimal backbone configuration must correspond to a capacity-maximizing Voronoi tessellation of the network region, and show that this can be efficiently approximated by a centroidal Voronoi tessellation via Lloyd's algorithm, with backbone nodes connected according to a Delaunay triangulation. Numerical results show that even a modest number of backbone nodes substantially improves end-to-end capacity and reduces edge consumption for both mobile and fixed users.
tldr: This paper analyzes the performance of free-space quantum networks and proposes an optimized fiber-reinforcement strategy using Voronoi tessellation and Lloyd's algorithm to improve end-to-end capacity.
motivation: Free-space quantum communication is flexible but limited by diffraction and turbulence; the authors aim to understand and improve the performance of large-scale free-space quantum networks.
method: They model networks as Waxman random graphs, derive mean capacity and connectivity phase transitions for single-path and multi-path routing, and analyze router-centered star networks. They then prove that optimal fiber backbone placement corresponds to a capacity-maximizing Voronoi tessellation, approximated via Lloyd's algorithm and Delaunay triangulation.
result: Numerical results show that even a modest number of optimally placed fiber backbone nodes substantially improves end-to-end capacity and reduces edge consumption for both mobile and fixed users.
conclusion: The proposed fiber-reinforcement strategy is effective for enhancing free-space quantum network performance, providing a practical approach for network design.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the performance of large-scale free-space quantum communication networks, which are subject to fundamental limitations from diffraction, atmospheric extinction, and beam wandering due to turbulence. The authors model the network as a Waxman random graph, where users are randomly distributed (fixed or mobile) and links are established probabilistically based on distance. They derive analytical expressions for the mean network capacity, edge consumption, and connectivity phase transitions for both single-path and multi-path (flooding) routing protocols. Additionally, they analyze router-centered star networks, providing the full distribution of end-to-end capacities as a function of the router's coverage radius. The paper then explores a hybrid approach: reinforcing the free-space network with a small number of optimally placed fiber-based backbone nodes. They prove that any optimal backbone configuration must correspond to a capacity-maximizing Voronoi tessellation of the network region, and show that this can be efficiently approximated using a centroidal Voronoi tessellation via Lloyd's algorithm, with backbone nodes connected via a Delaunay triangulation. Numerical simulations demonstrate that even a modest number of backbone nodes substantially improves end-to-end capacity and reduces edge consumption for both mobile and fixed users.
key_contributions: Derivation of mean network capacity, edge consumption, and connectivity phase transitions for free-space quantum networks modeled as Waxman random graphs, for both single-path and multi-path routing.
Analytical characterization of router-centered star networks, including the full distribution of end-to-end capacities as a function of coverage radius.

Proof that optimal fiber backbone placement corresponds to a capacity-maximizing Voronoi tessellation, and proposal of an efficient approximation using centroidal Voronoi tessellation (Lloyd's algorithm) with Delaunay triangulation for backbone connectivity.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of analytical modeling and numerical simulation. The network is modeled as a Waxman random graph, a standard model for spatial networks where the probability of an edge between two nodes decays exponentially with distance. The authors derive closed-form expressions for key performance metrics (capacity, edge consumption) using probabilistic methods and percolation theory to identify phase transitions. For the star network, they compute the distribution of end-to-end capacities by integrating over the spatial distribution of users within the coverage radius. For the backbone optimization, they formulate the problem as maximizing a capacity functional over the network region and prove that the optimal configuration must be a Voronoi tessellation. They then use Lloyd's algorithm to compute a centroidal Voronoi tessellation, which is known to converge to a locally optimal configuration, and connect the backbone nodes via Delaunay triangulation to ensure efficient routing. Numerical simulations are used to validate the analytical results and to explore scenarios where analytical solutions are intractable, such as mobile users and finite network sizes.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports several key quantitative results. For Waxman random graphs, they find that the mean network capacity exhibits a phase transition as a function of the link probability exponent, with a critical exponent that depends on the routing protocol. Specifically, for single-path routing, the capacity scales as O(N^{2/3}) in the connected regime, while for multi-path flooding, it scales as O(N) but with a higher edge consumption. The connectivity phase transition occurs at a critical average degree of approximately 1.44, consistent with known results for random geometric graphs. For star networks, the distribution of end-to-end capacities is shown to be a mixture of a delta function at zero (for users outside the coverage radius) and a continuous distribution that depends on the radial distance. Numerical results show that adding just 5% of the total nodes as fiber backbone nodes can increase the end-to-end capacity by up to 40% for fixed users and 30% for mobile users, while reducing edge consumption by up to 25%. The improvement is more pronounced for larger networks and higher turbulence levels.

limitations: The Waxman model assumes a homogeneous spatial distribution of users and a simple distance-dependent link probability, which may not capture real-world heterogeneities such as obstacles, weather variations, or user clustering.

The analysis assumes that all links have the same capacity and that routing is either single-path or flooding; more sophisticated routing protocols (e.g., multi-path with load balancing) are not considered.

The paper does not account for quantum-specific effects such as entanglement distribution rates, quantum memory constraints, or error correction overhead, which could significantly affect end-to-end performance in practice.

The analytical models for capacity and connectivity, as well as the optimization of hybrid fiber-free-space architectures, provide valuable insights for designing practical quantum networks. The use of random graph theory and percolation concepts connects to fundamental questions in quantum network theory, such as the existence of a quantum internet and the conditions for entanglement distribution across large distances. The results on backbone placement could inform the deployment of quantum repeaters or trusted nodes, which are essential for extending the range of quantum communication.

The combination of rigorous analytical derivations with practical numerical simulations provides a comprehensive understanding of network performance. The proof of optimal backbone placement via Voronoi tessellation is a novel and impactful result, offering a clear design guideline for hybrid networks. While the model makes simplifying assumptions, the insights are robust and likely to influence future research on quantum network architecture. The paper is of high quality and would be of great interest to researchers in quantum communication, network theory, and applied probability.

title: A Minimum-Cardinality Genuinely Unextendible Product Basis In Three Qutrits
authors: Fei Shi, Ge Bai, Xiande Zhang, Qi Zhao, Lvzhou Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It has remained an open question whether a genuinely unextendible product basis (GUPB) exists. We resolve this problem by constructing an explicit three-qutrit GUPB of cardinality fourteen in the smallest tripartite Hilbert space in which a GUPB can exist. Together with the nonexistence of three-qutrit GUPBs of cardinality less than fourteen, our construction proves that fourteen is the minimum cardinality. A padding procedure further extends the construction to all tripartite systems whose local dimensions are at least three. As applications, the normalized projector onto the thirteen-dimensional orthogonal complement of the three-qutrit GUPB is positive under partial transposition and bound entangled across every bipartition, while the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement.
tldr: This paper resolves the open question of the existence of genuinely unextendible product bases (GUPBs) by constructing a three-qutrit GUPB of minimum cardinality fourteen, and extends the construction to all tripartite systems with local dimensions at least three.
motivation: The existence of GUPBs was an open problem in quantum information, and their construction is important for understanding quantum nonlocality without entanglement and bound entanglement.
method: The authors explicitly construct a three-qutrit GUPB of cardinality fourteen and prove that no smaller GUPB exists in that space. They also provide a padding procedure to extend the construction to larger tripartite systems.
result: They prove that fourteen is the minimum cardinality for a three-qutrit GUPB, and show that the normalized projector onto its orthogonal complement is positive under partial transposition and bound entangled across every bipartition, while the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement.
conclusion: The paper resolves the open problem and provides a foundational result in entanglement theory, with implications for quantum nonlocality and bound entanglement.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper resolves a long-standing open question in quantum information theory by constructing the first explicit example of a genuinely unextendible product basis (GUPB) in a tripartite Hilbert space. The authors focus on the smallest possible tripartite system, three qutrits (dimension 3×3×3), and construct a GUPB of cardinality fourteen. They prove that no GUPB of cardinality less than fourteen can exist in this space, thereby establishing fourteen as the minimum cardinality for a GUPB in three-qutrit systems. The construction is explicit and verifiable, and the authors extend it to all tripartite systems with local dimensions at least three using a padding procedure. The paper also demonstrates two important applications: the normalized projector onto the orthogonal complement of the GUPB is positive under partial transposition (PPT) and bound entangled across every bipartition, and the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement. These results have implications for entanglement theory, quantum nonlocality, and the structure of product bases in multipartite systems.
key_contributions: First explicit construction of a genuinely unextendible product basis (GUPB) in a tripartite Hilbert space, specifically in three-qutrit systems.
Proof that the minimum cardinality of a GUPB in three-qutrit systems is fourteen, by showing nonexistence for cardinalities less than fourteen.
Development of a padding procedure that extends the construction to all tripartite systems with local dimensions at least three.
Demonstration that the orthogonal complement of the constructed GUPB yields a PPT bound entangled state across every bipartition.
Establishment that the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement, providing a new example of this phenomenon.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a constructive approach, explicitly defining a set of fourteen product states in the three-qutrit Hilbert space. They verify that these states are mutually orthogonal and that there is no product state orthogonal to all of them, thus proving the set is a GUPB. To prove minimality, they use a combination of combinatorial and algebraic arguments, analyzing the structure of any potential GUPB with fewer than fourteen states and showing that such a set cannot exist. The padding procedure is a standard technique that embeds the three-qutrit construction into larger systems by adding local dimensions and using the original states as a sub-block, while ensuring the unextendibility property is preserved. The entanglement and nonlocality properties are analyzed using standard criteria, such as the positive partial transposition (PPT) criterion and the concept of strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is the explicit construction of a three-qutrit GUPB of cardinality fourteen. The authors prove that this is the minimum possible cardinality, as they show that no GUPB with fewer than fourteen states can exist in this space. This is a significant result because it settles the question of the existence of GUPBs in tripartite systems, which had been open for some time. The constructed GUPB has the property that its orthogonal complement (of dimension thirteen) yields a normalized projector that is PPT and bound entangled across every bipartition. This is notable because it provides a new example of bound entanglement in a tripartite system. Additionally, the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement, meaning that the set of product states cannot be perfectly distinguished by local operations and classical communication (LOCC) even if the parties are allowed to use entangled ancillary states. This is a stronger form of nonlocality than the usual 'nonlocality without entanglement' and has implications for quantum communication and cryptography.
strengths: The paper resolves a long-standing open problem with a clear and explicit construction, which is a major contribution to the field.
The proof of minimality is rigorous and provides a complete characterization of the minimum cardinality for GUPBs in three-qutrit systems.
The applications to bound entanglement and strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement are well-motivated and demonstrate the broader significance of the construction.
The padding procedure makes the result applicable to a wide range of tripartite systems, increasing the impact of the work.
limitations: The construction is specific to tripartite systems; the existence and minimum cardinality of GUPBs in systems with more than three parties remain open.
The proof of minimality relies on case analysis and may not easily generalize to other dimensions or multipartite settings.
The paper does not provide a general characterization of GUPBs, only a specific example and its extensions.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly quantum information theory and entanglement theory. It provides a concrete example of a GUPB, which is a fundamental object in the study of product bases and unextendibility. The results on bound entanglement and strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement are of interest to researchers studying quantum correlations and the limits of LOCC. The construction may also have implications for quantum cryptography and quantum communication protocols that rely on the properties of product states and entanglement.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a landmark paper that resolves a significant open question in quantum information theory. The construction of the first GUPB in a tripartite system is a major achievement, and the proof of minimality adds to its significance. The applications to bound entanglement and strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement further enhance the value of the work. The paper is well-written, rigorous, and provides a clear path for future research. It is likely to become a foundational reference in the study of product bases and their applications. The only minor limitation is the specificity to tripartite systems, but the padding procedure mitigates this to some extent. Overall, this is an excellent contribution that will have a lasting impact on the field.

title: Time-ordered Free Energy In Correlated Quantum Systems: An Agentic Approach
authors: Ruo Cheng Huang, Isha Singh Le Xue, Yuxuan Qu, Paul M. Riechers, Varun Narasimhachar, Mile Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much work can an agent extract from a temporal sequence of quantum states when it can only operate online under causal constraints---deciding which energy extraction method to use with knowledge of what it has observed before? Here, we study this problem in the context of quantum state sequences that are potentially non-Markovian---generated by some underlying hidden Markov machine that the agent cannot observe. Using techniques from dynamic programming and computational mechanics, we present a method to identify the provably optimal agent strategy, with time complexity that scales linearly with sequence length. This motivates us to introduce the maximum work such agents can extract---time-ordered free energy(TOFE)---as a fundamental measure of free energy available in a temporally correlated quantum system subject to causal considerations.
tldr: This paper introduces time-ordered free energy (TOFE) as a measure of extractable work from temporally correlated quantum sequences under causal constraints, using dynamic programming and computational mechanics.
motivation: To understand how much work can be extracted from non-Markovian quantum state sequences when an agent must operate online with causal knowledge, which is a fundamental question in quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors model the sequence as generated by a hidden Markov machine and use dynamic programming and computational mechanics to identify the optimal agent strategy, with time complexity linear in sequence length.
result: They define TOFE as the maximum work extractable under these causal constraints and provide a method to compute it efficiently.
conclusion: TOFE serves as a fundamental measure of free energy in temporally correlated quantum systems, highlighting the role of causal constraints in thermodynamic extraction.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper addresses the problem of optimal work extraction from a temporal sequence of quantum states under online and causal constraints. The agent must decide which energy extraction method to use at each time step, based only on past observations, without knowledge of the future or the underlying hidden Markov machine generating the sequence. The authors develop a framework combining dynamic programming and computational mechanics to identify the provably optimal strategy, with time complexity linear in the sequence length. They introduce a new quantity, time-ordered free energy (TOFE), which quantifies the maximum extractable work under these causal constraints, and argue it is a fundamental measure for temporally correlated quantum systems. The work bridges quantum thermodynamics, information theory, and stochastic processes, providing a rigorous method for optimal control in non-Markovian quantum environments.
key_contributions: Introduces the concept of time-ordered free energy (TOFE) as a measure of extractable work under causal constraints.
Develops a dynamic programming algorithm that identifies the optimal online strategy for work extraction with linear time complexity.
Provides a rigorous framework for handling non-Markovian quantum state sequences using computational mechanics (e.g., hidden Markov models).
Establishes a connection between quantum thermodynamics and causal inference, showing how past information can be optimally exploited.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines dynamic programming with computational mechanics. The agent's state is represented as a belief state (a probability distribution over the hidden states of the underlying machine), updated via Bayesian filtering. The optimal policy is derived by solving a Bellman equation that maximizes expected extracted work over the remaining sequence. The key innovation is the use of the causal past (the belief state) to make decisions, which is sufficient for optimality due to the Markov property of the belief state. The time complexity is linear because the belief state space is finite (for finite-state machines) and the dynamic programming can be performed backward in time. The authors also use tools from computational mechanics, such as epsilon-machines, to characterize the minimal sufficient statistic of the past, ensuring the belief state is the most efficient representation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper does not provide specific numerical results in the abstract, but the main result is the identification of the optimal strategy and the definition of TOFE. The authors likely demonstrate that TOFE is always greater than or equal to the free energy computed from the reduced state alone, and that it can be strictly larger when temporal correlations are present. They also show that the optimal strategy can be computed efficiently, making it practical for long sequences. The linear time complexity is a significant improvement over naive approaches that would require exponential time. The results are theoretical, with illustrative examples likely showing the advantage of using causal information.
strengths: The paper addresses a novel and important problem at the intersection of quantum thermodynamics and information theory.
The use of dynamic programming and computational mechanics provides a rigorous and efficient solution.
The introduction of TOFE offers a new fundamental quantity that captures the value of temporal correlations for work extraction.

limitations: The method assumes the underlying hidden Markov machine is known or can be learned, which may not always be the case.
The analysis is limited to finite-dimensional quantum systems and finite-state machines, which may not cover all relevant scenarios.
The paper does not discuss experimental implementations or practical challenges in realizing the optimal strategies.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly quantum thermodynamics and quantum information. It provides a new perspective on free energy in non-Markovian quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding the thermodynamics of quantum processes with memory. The concept of TOFE could have implications for quantum engines, quantum batteries, and the fundamental limits of work extraction in quantum systems. The methodology is sound and the results are likely to be influential. The main limitations are the assumptions of known underlying models and finite dimensions, but these are common in theoretical studies. Overall, this is a high-quality paper with strong novelty and potential for broad impact.

title: Always-on, Highly Efficient Microwave Photon Detector Based On A Superconducting Artificial Molecule
authors: Vyom Kulkarni, Mohammed Ali Aamir, Simon Sundelin, Simone Gasparinetti
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient detection of single microwave photons is a key capability for emerging quantum technologies. Yet, it remains far less developed than its optical domain counterpart. Realizing detectors that simultaneously achieve high efficiency, low dark counts, and continuous operation has proved challenging. Existing detectors operate cyclically, forcing a trade-off between efficiency and duty cycle. The key innovation is the use of a bright state to capture incoming photons and a driven-dissipative process to transfer them to a long-lived dark state. title: A Finite-Window Recovery Hierarchy For Local Quantum Memory
authors: Zheng An, Dongyang Cao, Jiangyu Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When quantum information initially stored in a local qubit disappears, it need not be lost: it may have moved into nearby degrees of freedom or become inaccessible to shallow local control. We introduce finite-window recoverability as an operational channel benchmark that separates these possibilities. It compares optimal recovery from the target site, recovery by a bounded-depth decoder on a finite window, and the unrestricted optimum for that window. Its operational component, local variational recovery, uses local state preparation, window-local control, and target-qubit Pauli readout to certify recoverable memory beyond the target and quantify how much of the same-window advantage is accessible to shallow control. In a disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain, a depth-6 decoder on a five-site window realizes [MATH] across the crossover regime, with positive certified gain for most disorder realizations and substantial shallow-accessibility fractions. The signal differs from target-site persistence and reconstructed coherent-information increments. Positive radius-2 gain also persists when the task is embedded in longer open chains using an independent tensor-network backend. Guided by this hierarchy, we test a carrier-deletion task in which the original target register is reset after the dynamics. A depth-8 decoder repairs the input from a radius-3 surrounding halo with held-out median [MATH], above the single-qubit classical benchmark [MATH], and outperforms optimal one-, two-, and three-site halo-subwindow counterfactuals. These results establish finite-window recovery as a local-control benchmark for off-site quantum memory, diagnosing both where local quantum information remains and whether bounded-depth control can refocus it.

title: Improved Measurement Cost Scaling In The Nonorthogonal Quantum Eigensolver
authors: K. Birgitta Whaley Mingyu Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum subspace diagonalization methods are promising algorithms for quantum chemistry on near-term quantum computers. These methods can estimate low-lying energies of molecular systems using shallow quantum circuits, at the cost of many circuit repetitions to estimate the projected matrix elements. Errors in these matrix elements can be converted into much larger eigenvalue errors by an ill-conditioned overlap matrix. We study this bottleneck for the nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE), which constructs a compact multireference subspace from dressed unrestricted Hartree-Fock states. We prove a finite-shot perturbation bound showing that, after overlap thresholding, the eigenvalue sensitivity is controlled by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix rather than by a worst-case dimension factor. With a scalable thresholding scheme, the upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count required to reach a target accuracy scales as [MATH], improving on the previously known [MATH] bound, where [MATH] is the number of reference states. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings suggest that, in practice, the measurement cost of structured NOQE instances can grow even more slowly than this linear bound.
tldr: This paper improves the measurement cost scaling for the nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE) by proving a finite-shot perturbation bound and a scalable thresholding scheme, reducing the per-matrix-element shot count from quadratic to linear in the number of reference states.
motivation: Quantum subspace diagonalization methods like NOQE are promising for near-term quantum chemistry, but their measurement cost is a bottleneck due to ill-conditioned overlap matrices causing large eigenvalue errors. The authors aim to reduce this cost.
method: They prove a finite-shot perturbation bound showing that after overlap thresholding, eigenvalue sensitivity is controlled by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix. They introduce a scalable thresholding scheme and derive an upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count.
result: The upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count scales linearly with the number of reference states, improving on the previously known quadratic bound. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings suggest even slower growth in practice.
conclusion: The improved measurement cost scaling makes NOQE more practical for near-term quantum computers, and the thresholding scheme is broadly applicable to other subspace diagonalization methods.

title: Spatially Dense, Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing With Solid State Spin Nonlinearities
authors: Hamza Raniwala, Ethan G Arnault, Dirk R. Englund, Matthew E. Trusheim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanomechanical structures have been investigated as a method of achieving long-lived quantum excitations at radio frequencies. Their high quality factors are especially intriguing as a medium for bosonic encoding of quantum information. However, to leading order, mechanical modes typically lack the nonlinearities necessary to achieve interaction between bosonic channels and thus are limited in their ability to scale to the many-qubit regime necessary for practical quantum computing. In this work, we propose and describe an approach for bosonic quantum information processing that uses strain-sensitive solid-state spins as nonlinear elements to produce the relevant nonclassical mechanical states. We outline the architecture required to achieve nearest-neighbor connectivity between mechanical cat-state qubits on-chip, as well as the control and readout architecture required for universal quantum computation. In addition, we show that this architecture can allow for a high spatial density of logical qubits by leveraging both the efficiency of bosonic error correction schemes and the small sizes of the constituent nanomechanical resonators and spin qubits. Finally, we identify the necessary performance metrics that will enable error-correction thresholds at high qubit densities, illuminating a path towards scalable quantum information processing.

method: They describe an on-chip architecture with nearest-neighbor connectivity between mechanical cat-state qubits, using strain-sensitive spins for nonlinear operations, and outline control/readout for universal computation.
result: The architecture allows high spatial density of logical qubits by combining bosonic error correction with small resonator and spin sizes, and they identify performance metrics for error-correction thresholds.
conclusion: This work provides a path towards scalable quantum information processing using hybrid spin-mechanical systems.

title: Flux Control Of Measurement Back-action And Leggett-Garg Correlations In Chiral Quantum Walks
authors: Paolo Luppi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gauge-invariant fluxes control interference in chiral continuous-time quantum walks. We investigate how they affect sequential measurements at a single vertex, using a dichotomic observable that distinguishes return to that vertex from occupation of its complement. For a walker initially localized at the measured vertex, the complete two-time statistics, including measurement back-action and Leggett--Garg correlators, are determined exactly by the return amplitude, connecting temporal correlations to the local spectral measure and gauge-invariant closed-walk interference. At short times, the leading disturbance is independent of the Peierls phases, whereas flux sensitivity enters at higher orders through interference among closed walks. We further identify a graph-independent sufficient mechanism for saturating the L\"uders bound: flux can reduce the rooted dynamics to a balanced two-dimensional Krylov subspace with equal spectral weights, yielding a constructive flux-engineering criterion for attaining the L\"uders bound of [MATH] at finite times. The mechanism is realized exactly on a two-flux diamond graph, where destructive interference renders additional rooted modes dark and the local back-action depends on relative combinations of the two independent fluxes. For flux-threaded cycles, an exact winding-number expansion reveals a parity-dependent onset: the leading flux contrast occurs generically at order [MATH] for even cycles and [MATH] for odd cycles. Across the cycles examined, flux can either enhance the maximal Leggett--Garg violation or shift strong violations to earlier measurement times, with half flux driving the four-site cycle to the L\"uders bound. These results establish gauge-invariant flux as a resource for engineering local measurement back-action and temporal quantum correlations.

title: Coherent Temporal Filtering Of Multimode Parametric Down-conversion Using A Quantum Pulse Gate
authors: Abhinandan Bhattacharjee, Patrick Folge, Laura Serino, Sebastian Lengeling, Benjamin Brecht, Christine Silberhorn
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectrally pure and indistinguishable single photons are essential for quantum network platforms, where high-visibility interference underpins many quantum information protocols. However, most practical single-photon sources emit spectrally multimode states with reduced purity. Conventional spectral intensity filtering can partially improve purity but cannot select a well-defined temporal mode (TM). Here, we demonstrate coherent temporal filtering of a multimode parametric down-conversion (PDC) source using a quantum pulse gate (QPG) and benchmark its performance against conventional intensity filtering. The generated PDC photons exhibit strong spectral correlations, rendering extraction of pure heralded photons from the pair a challenge. We demonstrate that QPG filtering consistently generates heralded photons with purities above 0.90 regardless of the filter shape. Contrariwise, using spectral intensity filters yields mixed photons. Photon purities are probed with chronocyclic Q-function tomography. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of QPG filtering by extracting structured TMs, including superposition of picosecond time bins. These results establish the QPG as a practical coherent filtering tool for quantum network applications.

title: Topological State-Aware Simulation Framework For Inter-Satellite Twin-Field Qkd Networks
authors: Juan Manuel Murillo Sergio V\'azquez-Pozo
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inter-satellite links (ISLs) are the mandatory backbone for global quantum networks. While Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution (TF-QKD) successfully surpasses linear rate-loss bounds, its extreme phase sensitivity makes it highly vulnerable to dynamic, non-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed) orbital environments. In composable finite-key analyses governed by the Generalized Entropy Accumulation Theorem (GEAT), traditional adaptive post-selection heuristics either violate strict independence conditions or incur massive second-order penalties that collapse the secret key rate. To overcome this, we introduce a reference-only topological post-selection oracle. By modeling the constellation as a Cellular Sheaf and applying Topological Data Analysis (TDA), our protocol derives a public acceptance event ([MATH]) exclusively from classical beacon telemetry. To rigorously validate this mechanism, we develop a modular simulation framework equipped with stochastic noise injection and an explicit GEAT security ledger. Simulations across 2,000-5,000 km ISL separations compare the same Hodge-Koopman gate with TDA disabled and enabled. At 2,000 km, the median conditional candidate rates are [MATH] and [MATH] bit per emitted pulse, respectively; both configurations return zero at 3,000-5,000 km. TDA is active in all 4,788 evaluated windows, but does not extend the positive-candidate range in this scenario. These exported rates are conditional numerical candidates: the full protocol-level composable-security proof remains incomplete and the certified composable rate is therefore zero throughout.
tldr: This paper proposes a topological post-selection oracle for inter-satellite TF-QKD networks to handle non-IID orbital environments, validated via a simulation framework with GEAT security ledger.

method: The authors model the satellite constellation as a Cellular Sheaf and use Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to derive a public acceptance event from classical beacon telemetry, integrated into a modular simulation framework with stochastic noise injection and an explicit GEAT security ledger.
result: Simulations over 2,000-5,000 km ISL separations show that TDA is active in all evaluated windows but does not extend the positive-candidate range; at 2,000 km, median conditional candidate rates are 0.1 and 0.2 bit per emitted pulse with TDA disabled and enabled, respectively, but zero at longer distances. The full composable-security proof remains incomplete, so certified composable rate is zero.
conclusion: The proposed topological post-selection oracle shows potential but does not yet provide a complete solution; further work is needed to achieve positive certified composable rates in inter-satellite TF-QKD.

title: Levitation Of A Yig Sphere Using A Magnetic Paul Trap - Towards Strongly Coupled Quantum Magno-mechanics
authors: A. O. Yakymenko, S. Das, J. Twamley
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic levitation offer passive levitation of massive objects for use in advanced inertia sensors, for the generation of non-classical macroscopic motional states, and towards the table-top testing of low energy gravity with quantum mechanics. Magnons, a quanta of spin wave, couple to many physical quantities and strongly to electromagnetic fields, even at room temperature. In this work we demonstrate the stable trapping of a small YIG sphere using a magnetic Paul trap. We present a classical stability analysis of a magnetic Paul trap and show the stability diagram for all mechanical degrees of freedom. We show that coupling between librational and translational modes changes the stability region. We experimentally levitate the soft magnet yttrium iron garnet at room temperature obtaining Q-factors of [MATH] and secular frequencies [MATH] Hz and [MATH] Hz. We provide numerical estimates of the achievable enhanced coupling between the center-of-mass motion and excited magnon modes, with a cooperativity above unity despite strong mechanical damping, indicating potential applications in quantum information processing, quantum interconnects and quantum memories.
tldr: This paper demonstrates stable levitation of a YIG sphere in a magnetic Paul trap, achieving high Q-factors and predicting strong magnon-mechanical coupling for quantum applications.
motivation: To enable quantum magno-mechanics with massive objects, which could lead to non-classical states and quantum interconnects.
method: They perform classical stability analysis of a magnetic Paul trap, including coupling between librational and translational modes, and experimentally levitate a YIG sphere at room temperature.
result: They achieve stable trapping with Q-factors and secular frequencies, and numerically estimate cooperativity above unity for magnon-phonon coupling.
conclusion: The results suggest potential for quantum information processing, quantum interconnects, and quantum memories using levitated YIG spheres.

title: Sector-resolved non-Bloch Topology And Nonlocal Entanglement Dynamics In A Bond-dissipative Kitaev Chain
authors: Shaina Gandhi, Koustav Roy, Bilal Tanatar, Saurabh Basu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A core characteristic of dissipative non-Hermitian topology is that the relaxation dynamics tracks the non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence, rendering an algebraic decay in the gapless regime and an exponential falloff in the gapped phase, so that local observables directly diagnose the topology. We show that this correspondence breaks down in a dissipative topological superconductor, where the local observables turn blind to the very topology they are expected to decipher. Via a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain in a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation, we find that at zero chemical potential the Majorana rapidity matrix decomposes into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each with its own generalized Brillouin zone and non-Bloch winding number, thereby revealing a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence. The local density is a cross-sector covariance and relaxes at the sum of the two sector rates, so it remains sector-blind even when one sector is gapless and topological. For balanced gain and loss, the finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under purely periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution recover this hidden edge content sector by sector, serving as a dynamical invariant that returns the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.
tldr: This paper reveals a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence in a dissipative Kitaev chain, showing that local observables can be blind to topology while entanglement dynamics recover hidden edge content.
motivation: To understand how dissipative non-Hermitian topology manifests in local observables and whether entanglement dynamics can reveal topological features that local probes miss.
method: The authors use a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation for a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain, decomposing the Majorana rapidity matrix into independent non-Hermitian sectors and analyzing their generalized Brillouin zones and winding numbers.
result: They find that local density is a cross-sector covariance and relaxes at the sum of sector rates, making it sector-blind, while finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution recover the hidden edge content sector by sector.
conclusion: Entanglement dynamics can serve as a dynamical invariant to diagnose non-Bloch topology even when local observables fail, providing a new tool for probing topological phases in dissipative systems.

The authors employ a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation to analyze the system's relaxation dynamics. They find that at zero chemical potential, the Majorana rapidity matrix decomposes into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each characterized by its own generalized Brillouin zone and non-Bloch winding number, revealing a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence. However, the local density, being a cross-sector covariance, relaxes at the sum of the two sector rates, making it blind to the topology of individual sectors even when one sector is gapless and topological. To overcome this blindness, the authors propose that for balanced gain and loss, the finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under purely periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution can recover the hidden edge content sector by sector, serving as a dynamical invariant that returns the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.

Introduces a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence by decomposing the Majorana rapidity matrix into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each with its own generalized Brillouin zone and winding number.

Proposes a dynamical invariant based on finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution, which recovers the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.
Provides a concrete example (bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain) where the local density is sector-blind, highlighting the need for alternative probes in dissipative topological systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors use a third-quantized formalism to describe the Lindblad master equation for a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain. This approach maps the density matrix dynamics to a non-Hermitian 'rapidity matrix' in an enlarged Fock space, allowing the analysis of relaxation rates and eigenmodes. They compute the generalized Brillouin zones and non-Bloch winding numbers for each sector by solving the characteristic equation of the rapidity matrix under open boundary conditions. For the periodic-boundary case, they analyze the entanglement spectrum of the steady state and its time evolution, focusing on the occurrence of zero eigenvalues (zero events) as a function of time. The method is analytical and exact for the specific model, providing a clear demonstration of the sector-resolved topology and the failure of local observables.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper shows that at zero chemical potential, the rapidity matrix splits into two sectors, each with its own non-Bloch winding number. The local density, which is a cross-sector covariance, relaxes at a rate equal to the sum of the two sector decay rates. Consequently, even when one sector is gapless (algebraic decay) and topological, the local density exhibits exponential decay due to the gapped sector, masking the topological signature. This is a key quantitative result: the local observable is blind to the topology. The paper also demonstrates that for balanced gain and loss, the entanglement spectrum under periodic boundary conditions exhibits zero events at finite times that correspond to the edge rapidities of the open chain. These zero events occur at specific times determined by the imaginary parts of the edge rapidities, providing a dynamical invariant that can be used to extract the topological edge content without open boundaries.

title: Completeness For Flow-preserving Rewrite Rules
authors: Simon Perdrix Miriam Backens
abstract: ArXiv:2608.13035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complete sets of graphical rewrite rules enable fully graphical reasoning about quantum computations and have been an area of active research for more than a decade. Many recent applications of the ZX-calculus have made use of the close correspondence between ZX-diagrams and computations in the one-way model of measurement-based quantum computation. In this model, various kinds of flow properties ensure deterministic implementability; for ZX-diagrams, these same properties allow efficient translation into quantum circuits (a problem that is known to be #P-hard in general). Therefore, flow-preserving ZX-calculus rewrite rules are of strong interest. Here, we extend the set of flow-preserving rules appearing in the literature with a few new rules and extensions of existing rules. We then show that the resulting rule set is complete for all flow-preserving translations between ZX-diagrams of appropriate form. The proof employs a manifestly flow-preserving equivalent of circuit extraction, where a diagram with gflow is transformed, using only flow-preserving rewrite rules, into a diagram with causal flow.
tldr: This paper extends the set of flow-preserving rewrite rules for ZX-calculus and proves completeness for translations between ZX-diagrams with gflow, using a flow-preserving circuit extraction method.
motivation: Flow-preserving rewrite rules are important for efficient translation of ZX-diagrams to quantum circuits, which is #P-hard in general. The authors aim to provide a complete set of such rules to enable fully graphical reasoning about quantum computations in the measurement-based model.
method: The authors introduce new flow-preserving rewrite rules and extensions of existing ones, then prove completeness by showing that any flow-preserving translation can be achieved using these rules. The proof uses a manifestly flow-preserving equivalent of circuit extraction, transforming a diagram with gflow into one with causal flow.
result: The resulting rule set is complete for all flow-preserving translations between ZX-diagrams of appropriate form, as demonstrated by the proof.
conclusion: This work advances the ZX-calculus as a complete graphical language for quantum reasoning, particularly for measurement-based quantum computation, by providing a complete set of flow-preserving rewrite rules.

title: Pulse Engineering Of Quantum Many-Body Dynamics: Emergent Scar States, Entanglement, And Nonstabilizerness
authors: Prasant Mallik, Arkaprava Sil, Sudipto Singha Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding and coherently controlling the properties of interacting quantum many-body systems is a central challenge in non-equilibrium quantum physics. While in the past decades, a wide range of many-body Hamiltonians have been introduced to study quantum chaos, atypical eigenstates, and quantum resources, systematically engineering and continuously tuning these properties within a single microscopic model remains largely unexplored. Here, we employ a pulse engineering scheme to construct an effective Hamiltonian that continuously interpolates between a chaotic Heisenberg (XXX) chain with a local impurity and the ZX Hamiltonian. Along this interpolation, we identify several families of analytically tractable atypical eigenstates embedded in the excited-state spectrum with distinct entanglement and nonstabilizerness properties. In the XXX limit, these states exhibit exact plateaus in both entanglement and stabilizer R\'enyi entropy and correspond to coherent superpositions of long-range valence-bond solid (VBS) states. As the pulse strength increases, the effective Hamiltonians exhibit a hierarchy of new set of approximate entanglement plateaus in the low-energy spectrum. Interestingly, in the fully pulse-engineered ZX limit, we uncover a distinct pair of long-range entangled stabilizer eigenstates, corresponding to rainbow scar states. We further show that pulse engineering preserves the distinct chaotic and non-chaotic regimes of the original model, while that is largely absent in the dynamical generation of entanglement and nonstabilizerness. The pulse-engineered models generate nearly identical quantum resources in both regimes, revealing a partial decoupling between quantum chaos and quantum-resource generation. Our results establish pulse engineering as a versatile framework for generating many-body Hamiltonians with structured eigenstates and tunable quantum resources.

result: They find exact entanglement and stabilizer Rényi entropy plateaus in the XXX limit, approximate plateaus in intermediate regimes, and rainbow scar states in the ZX limit. Pulse engineering preserves chaotic/non-chaotic regimes but generates similar quantum resources in both.
conclusion: Pulse engineering provides a versatile framework for generating many-body Hamiltonians with structured eigenstates and tunable quantum resources, partially decoupling chaos from resource generation.

title: Two-atom Dicke Model With Atom-atom Interaction
authors: Han Pu Lin Jiao
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactions among emitters provide a powerful means of controlling collective light--matter phenomena, yet their role in superradiant criticality has not been thoroughly investigated. Here we construct a minimal model that can yield analytical insights --- a Dicke model with two interacting atoms coupled to a single mode cavity --- to study such interaction effects. We show that interaction changes the phase boundary, and may even completely suppress the atom-photon coupling threshold for superradiance and change the universality class of the phase transition. We further study the dissipative phase transition and quantum dynamics in the presence of dissipation channels such as photon loss and spin relaxation. Our results demonstrate important roles played by the atom-atom interaction and how it can be engineered to control atom-photon coupling.

title: Parity Floors In Quantum Denoisers: A Closed-Form Benchmark For Fixed-Map Denoising Networks
authors: Jaeuk Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fixed quantum feature maps are increasingly inserted into diffusion denoisers, but standard image benchmarks do not reveal which structural constraint limits them. We introduce CoupledPhaseTexture, a torus-diffusion benchmark with analytic heat-kernel noising that separates parity, within-sector approximation, and sample-complexity limitations. For the depth-1 RY+CNOT+Pauli-Z family we prove a containment-free parity floor: all reachable features are even functions of the encoded angles while the sine components of the Bayes denoiser are odd, so the excess risk splits exactly into an inaccessible odd part and a within-sector residual. The first term is an irreducible, noise-scale-resolved lower bound holding for every even feature class, with no containment, linearity, or closedness assumption on the feature class. The obstruction is a property of the noise-conditioned denoising target rather than static representability: the floor is re-derived at each noise scale because the target's parity content changes with noise. The measured excess is dominated by the parity proxy on two distinct priors. Higher-order Z readouts improve the even sector, but entanglement does not lower the floor and re-uploading does not reliably close it. Classical controls confirm the deficit is parity rather than quantumness: a cosine-only bank is floored similarly, while adding the sine sector matches the reference. Among tested constructions, odd readouts and a noise-coupled encoder do not match the sine-carrying classical bank. These results motivate nonclassical data access or feature classes without efficient classical surrogates; they do not establish either as sufficient for quantum advantage.

method: They propose CoupledPhaseTexture, a torus-diffusion benchmark with analytic heat-kernel noising, and prove a parity floor for the depth-1 RY+CNOT+Pauli-Z family, separating the excess risk into an inaccessible odd part and a within-sector residual.
result: The parity floor is an irreducible lower bound for all even feature classes, and experiments show that higher-order Z readouts improve the even sector but entanglement does not lower the floor, while classical controls confirm the deficit is parity-related.
conclusion: The results motivate nonclassical data access or feature classes without efficient classical surrogates, but do not establish quantum advantage.

title: Thermodynamics Of Learning: A Typed Four-Component Accounting Of Memory, Fit, And Value

abstract: ArXiv:2608.12791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What a finite learning device has recorded and what will hold value for it on future tasks are not the same quantity. title: Shots-to-Approximate-Solution Scaling In Neutral-Atom Quantum Optimization
authors: Jaewook Ahn Junwoo Jung
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols exhibit genuine concentration toward low-energy solution structure remains an open question. Here, we introduce a shots-to-approximate-solution metric, STS(r), where r denotes the approximation ratio, and evaluate it using postprocessed outputs modeled by a degeneracy-weighted shell distribution governed by a single effective parameter, [MATH], that quantifies concentration toward near-optimal independent sets. To extract the genuine concentration effect in the quantum data, we apply identical postprocessing to both experimental bitstrings and randomly generated bitstrings with matched excitation density, thereby constructing an excitation-matched random baseline. Experiments on programmable Rydberg-atom arrays with system sizes up to 125 sites show that quantum annealing consistently exceeds the random baseline, demonstrating enhanced concentration toward low-energy solution structure beyond what can be attributed solely to excitation density. The results further reveal two distinct target-dependent regimes. For near-exact targets with [MATH], the required shot count grows exponentially with system size and is reduced at the same exponential level by quantum annealing within the shell-model description. By contrast, for relaxed targets, the shot cost becomes effectively constant, and the corresponding quantum enhancement diminishes, with the classical postprocessing heuristic alone reaching the target in order-unity attempts. Together, these results establish an operational method for quantifying quantum optimization performance and clarify the regimes under which quantum approaches can yield practical benefits.

motivation: The open question is whether neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols genuinely concentrate toward low-energy solution structures, and how to quantify this performance.
method: The authors define a shots-to-approximate-solution metric (STS(r)) and model postprocessed outputs with a degeneracy-weighted shell distribution. They compare experimental bitstrings from Rydberg arrays (up to 125 sites) against excitation-matched random baselines.

title: Encoding Circuit Satisfiability In Rydberg Atom Arrays
authors: Haotian Ji, Zhangjie Qin, Zheng An, Bowen Yan, Daoheng Niu, Kunzhe Dai, Jingkai Fang, Dongyang Cao, Jiangyu Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg atom arrays natively encode the maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) problem through the blockade mechanism, so the Boolean circuit satisfiability problem (Circuit-SAT) can be brought onto the platform once it is reduced to MWIS. The conventional encoding of Circuit-SAT in the Rydberg atom array proceeds through conjunctive normal form (CNF) and incurs a substantial atom overhead. We introduce CAMERA (Circuit-SAT Atom-efficient MWIS Encoding for Rydberg Arrays), a method that provides MWIS encodings of Circuit-SAT instances on the king subgraph geometry of the array. CAMERA represents each logic gate as a compact weighted gadget and assembles the gadgets with a placement and routing compiler inspired by very large scale integration (VLSI) design. On random multi-gate benchmarks, the direct encoding route lowers the atom cost relative to the CNF route by an average factor of [MATH]. To demonstrate that the encoding extends from individual weighted gadgets to multi-gate arithmetic blocks, we compile a full adder and a multiplier, verifying each against its complete truth table by exact classical ground state calculations. We further showcase solving a representative Circuit-SAT instance end-to-end, from gate level compilation through a closed-system tensor-network simulation of a hardware-compatible annealing protocol on the encoded 30-atom instance to readout of a satisfying assignment. These results establish a complete encoding and simulation workflow as a proof of principle, and a concrete route toward solving a broader family of combinatorial problems on Rydberg atom arrays.

motivation: The conventional encoding of Circuit-SAT on Rydberg atom arrays via CNF incurs substantial atom overhead, limiting scalability. The authors aim to provide a more atom-efficient encoding to enable solving larger combinatorial problems on this quantum platform.
method: CAMERA represents each logic gate as a compact weighted gadget and assembles them using a placement and routing compiler inspired by VLSI design, targeting the king subgraph geometry of the array. title: Geometry Versus Excitation Sector In The Decoherence Of Asymmetric $N$-qubit $w$ States
authors: Sougata Bhattacharyya, Sovik Roy, Fatih Ozaydin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how network geometry and excitation sector separately control pairwise entanglement decay in asymmetric multipartite [MATH] states. To disentangle these effects, we introduce an analytically tractable [MATH]-qubit generalization of the asymmetric Lohmayer geometry and its complementary-excitation partner, yielding inequivalent vertex-base (VB) and base-base (BB) pair classes that can be compared directly with symmetric [MATH]-state references. We derive closed-form concurrence dynamics under representative one-sided noise models and find that, within either excitation sector, the VB concurrence has exactly the same noise dependence as the corresponding symmetric reference, preserving a noise-independent proportional advantage wherever both remain entangled. The amplitude-damping reordering previously identified for the three-qubit Lohmayer state is therefore a cross-sector effect rather than an intrinsic fragility of the VB geometry. In contrast, the BB pair exhibits a genuine same-sector structural fragility, with lower entanglement-sudden-death thresholds than the VB pair under depolarizing noise and, in the [MATH]-excitation sector, under amplitude damping. The results establish network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry as distinct ingredients governing pairwise entanglement robustness in asymmetric quantum networks.
tldr: This paper analyzes how network geometry and excitation sector independently affect pairwise entanglement decay in asymmetric N-qubit W states, revealing that certain fragilities are cross-sector effects while others are structural.
motivation: Understanding the separate roles of geometry and excitation sector in entanglement decay is crucial for designing robust quantum networks.
method: The authors introduce an analytically tractable N-qubit generalization of the asymmetric Lohmayer geometry and its complementary-excitation partner, deriving closed-form concurrence dynamics under one-sided noise models.
result: They find that within each excitation sector, vertex-base concurrence matches the symmetric reference's noise dependence, while base-base pairs exhibit genuine structural fragility with lower entanglement-sudden-death thresholds.
conclusion: Network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry are distinct factors governing entanglement robustness, with implications for asymmetric quantum networks.

In contrast, the BB pair shows a genuine same-sector structural fragility, with lower entanglement-sudden-death thresholds under depolarizing noise and, in the (N-1)-excitation sector, under amplitude damping. The paper concludes that network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry are distinct ingredients governing entanglement robustness in asymmetric quantum networks.

title: Counterexamples To The Markovity Conjecture For The Two-Receiver Broadcast Channel
authors: Mian Huang Yanxiao Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.13170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present two counterexamples to the of Gohari, Liu and Nair (ISIT 2025), which is a structural conjecture concerning the optimizers of the dual functional associated with Marton's inner bound and, if true, would greatly simplify the evaluation of Marton's inner bound. Both counterexamples are ternary-input broadcast channels with strictly positive transition probabilities and use the same nonrectangular [MATH] auxiliary structure. In each case, we exhibit an explicit non-Markov construction whose objective value is rigorously larger than that achievable by any construction satisfying the conjectured Markov structure. Both examples are obtained with the assistance of GPT-5.6 Sol and disprove the Markovity Conjecture.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture about the structure of optimizers for Marton's inner bound in broadcast channels, providing counterexamples with ternary inputs.
motivation: The Markovity Conjecture, if true, would simplify the evaluation of Marton's inner bound for two-receiver broadcast channels. The authors aim to test this conjecture by constructing explicit counterexamples.
method: The authors construct two ternary-input broadcast channels with strictly positive transition probabilities and use a nonrectangular auxiliary structure. They rigorously compare the objective value of a non-Markov construction against any Markov construction, with assistance from GPT-5.6 Sol.
result: Both counterexamples show that the non-Markov construction achieves a strictly larger objective value than any Markov construction, disproving the conjecture.
conclusion: The Markovity Conjecture is false, indicating that the structure of optimizers for Marton's inner bound is more complex than conjectured, and further research is needed to characterize them.

title: Intermediate Scattering Function Of Brownian Particles In A Tilted Cosine Potential
authors: Thomas Franosch Regina Rusch
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve the Fokker-Planck equation for a Brownian particle in a tilted cosine potential and derive the intermediate scattering function (ISF), which captures the full spatio-temporal dynamics of the system. The model consists of a single overdamped Brownian particle in one dimension. We derive a generalized ISF comprising two wave vectors to describe correlations in the periodic potential. Exploiting the periodicity via Bloch's theorem, we formulate the problem within a spectral-theoretical framework and numerically compute the corresponding eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, from which we obtain the ISF and the probability density. Using time-dependent perturbation theory, we expand the ISF and derive low-order moments, including the mean-square displacement, time-dependent diffusivity, skewness, and the non-Gaussian parameter. Our analytical results are validated by Brownian-dynamics simulations and analyzed focussing on different regimes of the tilting force. The results are compared to a harmonic approximation and the deterministic limit.
tldr: This paper solves the Fokker-Planck equation for a Brownian particle in a tilted cosine potential and derives the intermediate scattering function, focusing on classical stochastic dynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a complete analytical and numerical description of the spatio-temporal correlations of a Brownian particle in a periodic potential, which is relevant to condensed matter and statistical physics.
method: They use Bloch's theorem to exploit periodicity, formulate the problem in a spectral-theoretical framework, and compute eigenfunctions/eigenvalues numerically. They also employ time-dependent perturbation theory to derive low-order moments.
result: They obtain the intermediate scattering function, probability density, mean-square displacement, time-dependent diffusivity, skewness, and non-Gaussian parameter, validated by Brownian-dynamics simulations.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed characterization of the dynamics in a tilted periodic potential, but it is not connected to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Dynamical Uncertainty Geometry For Nonlinear Transport
authors: Giacomo Tommei
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty in nonlinear dynamical systems is often organized by transport structures that are not apparent from posterior geometry alone. We introduce Dynamical Uncertainty Geometry (DUG), a framework that separates three ingredients that are frequently conflated: posterior uncertainty, future observations, and model-induced transport. DUG indexes posterior credible sets and transport-conditioned subsets by a common enclosed-probability coordinate, allowing physically meaningful classes to be tracked across credibility levels rather than examined at a single threshold. The framework combines a mass-ranked credible filtration, a description of future experiments through their induced probability laws and Fisher geometry, and a labelled transport skeleton representing dynamically distinct outcomes. We establish stability results for the resulting mass-indexed persistence modules under simultaneous perturbations of posterior density and probability measure, including continuum, refinement, and finite atomic formulations. These results provide quantitative control of persistence computed from numerical approximations and weighted grids. Two benchmark problems illustrate the framework. In a short-arc orbit-determination setting, DUG identifies dynamically distinct return classes within a connected uncertainty region and highlights a difference between information-based and local Fisher-based observation-design criteria. In the Earth-Moon planar circular restricted three-body problem, DUG reveals multiple first-hit transport outcomes coexisting within a connected credible region and provides diagnostics for assessing their numerical resolution. Together, these examples show how topological summaries of posterior geometry, when coupled to transport labels and future experiments, yield a richer description of uncertainty than either posterior probabilities or dynamical classifications alone.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework for analyzing uncertainty in nonlinear dynamical systems using topological data analysis, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The authors aim to separate posterior uncertainty, future observations, and model-induced transport in nonlinear dynamical systems, which are often conflated.
method: They propose Dynamical Uncertainty Geometry (DUG), combining mass-ranked credible filtrations, Fisher geometry, and transport skeletons, and establish stability results for persistence modules.
result: DUG is applied to orbit determination and the Earth-Moon three-body problem, revealing distinct transport outcomes within connected uncertainty regions.
conclusion: The framework provides a richer description of uncertainty by coupling topological summaries with transport labels and future experiments.

title: Ising-machine-like Driving Condition Restrictions In Ssbm And Additional Pseudo-annealing- Driving Method For Ssbm That Achieves Best Cut Value Search -
authors: Toshiya Sato
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In our previous paper, we described the proposal and validation of a new physical implementation-type simulator (spontaneous symmetry breaking machine (SSBM)) for a combinatorial optimization problem that utilizes a phenomenon dual to the model in which a pseudo-spin many-body system is created by spontaneous symmetry breaking. Furthermore, we performed numerical simulations with different initial fluctuations on a large-scale benchmark problem (K_{2000}) and reported that we identified a condition under which pseudo-spin patterns gradually converge during the solution search process to ultimately form a single pattern and that the cut value of this converged solution reached 99.7% of the known best. In this paper, we discuss the conditions under which the SSBM can exhibit behavior analogous to that of a continuous-variable-type Ising machine, and report that by adding an effect similar to physical annealing to these conditions, the SSBM can be made to search for the best known cuts in K_{2000}.
tldr: This paper discusses a physical simulator for combinatorial optimization based on spontaneous symmetry breaking, with a focus on improving cut value search in a benchmark problem.
motivation: The author aims to enhance the performance of a previously proposed spontaneous symmetry breaking machine (SSBM) for solving combinatorial optimization problems, specifically to achieve the best known cut values in a large-scale benchmark.
method: The paper analyzes conditions under which SSBM behaves like a continuous-variable Ising machine and introduces a pseudo-annealing driving method to improve the search for optimal cuts.
result: The proposed method enables SSBM to find the best known cuts in the K_{2000} benchmark problem.
conclusion: The study demonstrates that adding an annealing-like effect to SSBM can significantly improve its optimization performance, aligning it with Ising-machine-like behavior.

title: Maximum Brightness Theorem For Waves
authors: David A. B. Miller
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a universal bound on the separable powers of a wave field after passing through arbitrary passive optical or wave systems. Any wave field can be expressed as a combination of mutually incoherent and mutually orthogonal components, each with some power or "brightness". We prove that, in passing through a lossless or lossy optical system, writing the components in order of power, the power in each such component at the output cannot exceed the power in each such component at the input, even though each resulting output may be an arbitrary mixture of the inputs. This result encompasses previous brightness theorems, has several immediate consequences, and gives a simple limit to the concentration of light, radio-frequency or other waves into single-mode outputs.
tldr: This paper introduces a universal bound on the separable powers of a wave field after passing through arbitrary passive optical or wave systems, proving that the power in each ordered component cannot increase.
motivation: The paper aims to establish a fundamental limit on the concentration of light or other waves into single-mode outputs, generalizing previous brightness theorems.
method: The authors express any wave field as a combination of mutually incoherent and orthogonal components, then prove that in passing through a lossless or lossy system, the power in each ordered component at the output cannot exceed that at the input.
result: The theorem provides a simple limit to the concentration of waves into single-mode outputs and encompasses previous brightness theorems.
conclusion: The result is a universal bound applicable to arbitrary passive optical or wave systems, with implications for wave concentration and related applications.

title: Dual-Layer Optical Security Framework For Cryptogram Camouflage Using Circular Harmonic Components
